title: How to Pick a Web Design Partner Without Getting Ripped Off
excerpt: How to choose a web design partner in Kenya: what to ask, which red flags to watch for, how to compare quotes fairly, and how to get a website that actually brings in customers.
author: Noon Studio Africa

content.text: Every month, a Kenyan business owner signs a website contract and ends up with a slow template, a silent developer, and a bill that keeps growing. It is one of the most common ways small businesses waste money online.
The good news is that the pattern is easy to spot before you sign. This guide shows you what to ask, what to avoid, and how to pick a partner who treats your money like their own.

items: The people who pitch your project should be the people who build it.
Fixed, written quotes beat hourly billing and vague estimates.
Ask who does the work before you ask how much it costs.
A partner who asks about your customers is a partner who cares about results.
Cheap is expensive. A KES 35,000 site that fails and gets rebuilt costs more than a proper build.

content.text: Why Small Businesses Get Burned
The pattern repeats itself because the incentives are wrong. Some studios sell work with senior people, then hand the delivery to whoever is cheapest to keep on payroll.
Others bill by the hour, which quietly rewards slow work and long email chains. None of this means these people are evil. It means the model is built for their benefit, not yours.

items: A salesperson sells you the dream, then disappears.
The person you met is not the person doing the work.
Revisions get billed as extra scope.
Communication happens through an account manager who knows less than you do.
The project drags on because time is money for them, not for you.

content.text: Once you know the pattern, you can check for it in one phone call. That call costs nothing. A bad contract costs six figures.
What to Look For in a Web Design Partner
Good partners are rare, but they share the same habits. Look for these five things and you will be hard to rip off.

items: The people who pitch are the people who build. Ask for names, not 'our team'.
Fixed pricing in writing. A clear scope and a clear quote, with no surprises.
They ask about your customers before they talk about colours.
They show work from the actual people you will work with.
They explain what happens after launch: support, updates, and who to call.

content.text: A partner who asks about your customers before talking about designs is telling you where their attention is. That is the single best signal there is.
The Five Questions That Separate Pros From Pretenders

items: Who will actually do the work? Get names, not 'our team'.
Who do I talk to during the project? Direct contact beats account-manager relays.
How are revisions billed? Fixed scope beats hourly surprises.
Can I see work from the people I will work with?
How long did a similar project take? Vague answers mean handoffs.

content.text: One honest conversation answers all of it. If the pitch features senior people and the delivery team is anonymous, you already know the pattern.
Do not be shy about asking. Good studios answer happily, because they have nothing to hide. Evasion is a signal, and it is cheaper to read it before you sign.
How to Compare Quotes Fairly
When three studios quote you KES 80,000, KES 250,000 and KES 600,000, they are not selling the same thing. Compare scope, not just price.

rows: A template with stock photos. Fine as a business card, rarely brings customers.
Custom design, SEO foundation, analytics, and support. The serious tier.
E-commerce, payments, inventory, or custom apps. Bigger build, longer timeline.

content.text: The cheapest option often costs the most in the long run. A KES 35,000 template that fails and gets replaced by a KES 350,000 build is a KES 385,000 website.
What Good Communication Feels Like
You will know a good partner within the first week. Questions get answered in hours, not days. Feedback lands with the person who can act on it.
When something needs a decision, there is no chain of command to climb. You are not one of fifty launches that month. Your project is the project.

FAQ

items.q: How much should a small business spend on a website in Kenya?
items.a: For a serious custom site that brings in customers, budget KES 120,000-500,000. Template sites from KES 15,000 exist, but they rarely generate leads and often get rebuilt within a year.

items.q: Is it safe to hire a freelancer for a website?
items.a: Some freelancers are excellent. The risk is the one-person dependency: if they disappear, so does your site. Ask about handover, hosting access, and who holds the login details.

items.q: Should I pay the full amount upfront?
items.a: Be careful with 100% upfront payments. A sensible structure is a deposit to start, a milestone payment, and the balance on launch. That protects both sides.

items.q: How do I know who will actually do my work?
items.a: Ask directly. A straight answer with names is a good sign. Evasion, 'our team', or 'our account manager will coordinate' is a warning.
Scope, price, timeline, revision limits, what happens after launch, and who owns the site, domain and content when the project ends. If a clause is missing, ask for it in writing.

content.text: Pick the Partner Who Does the Work
The choice is simple once you see it clearly. You can pay for a sales process and hope the work survives it, or you can work directly with the people building your site.
